name: Mouth breathing correction / myofunctional therapy

lead: Mouth breathing correction is a set of habits and exercises that push breathing through the nose and keep the tongue resting against the palate, sometimes with lip taping at night. People pursue it for a better airway and, they hope, a more defined jaw and better-developed face.

Proponents say tongue posture and nasal airflow shape the jaws and airway. Chronic mouth breathing in children has been proposed to influence dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face, though the relationship may run in both directions, and that support comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual models. Myofunctional therapy is studied for breathing and sleep apnea; studies of changing adult facial structure were not found in the sources reviewed.

paras: People practise tongue and lip exercises, hold a nasal-breathing habit during the day and sometimes tape the lips at night. It is often combined with treating nasal congestion, which is the usual cause of mouth breathing. Breathing changes are usually judged over weeks; facial claims play out over much longer.

The health effects of mouth taping have been little researched, according to encyclopedic sources. Persistent mouth breathing can reflect nasal obstruction or other conditions that merit assessment, and taping is generally not advised for people with blocked noses or untreated sleep apnea.

web.title: Mouth Taping For Better Sleep? Little Benefit, Lots Of Risk, Review Says - HealthDay

angle.text: Users practise nasal breathing, tongue posture and lip exercises, sometimes taping the lips at night, hoping for a better airway and a more defined jaw and face. Myofunctional therapy has been studied for breathing; the facial-structure link rests mainly on conceptual models.

lead: Mouth breathing correction is the practice of shifting breathing from the mouth to the nose and training the tongue, lips and jaw muscles to rest in what proponents call a proper posture. It includes orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT), a set of tongue, lip and swallowing exercises usually taught by a therapist, as well as habits such as nasal breathing and, in some communities, taping the lips closed during sleep [1][2][3]. People pursue it in the hope of a better-defined jaw and midface, a more closed mouth at rest, and better sleep, which they also link to how rested and healthy they look.

The facial case rests on the proposal that chronic mouth breathing in children influences dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face sometimes called long face syndrome, although Wikipedia notes the relationship may run in both directions [1]. In about 85 percent of cases mouth breathing is described as an adaptation to nasal congestion, and treatment focuses on any underlying obstruction and on building a nasal breathing habit [1]. On looksmax.org, OMT is presented as part of 'face maxxing' alongside tongue posture and jaw work [4].

Published trials of myofunctional therapy have mostly looked at sleep apnea, tongue thrust and open bite rather than facial appearance. Meta-analyses of adult sleep apnea patients report lower apnea-hypopnea index scores and less snoring and sleepiness after therapy [2][3], and small randomised trials have examined OMT in children and adults with open bite [5][6].

paras: About 85 percent of cases are attributed to nasal congestion, with less common causes including antrochoanal polyps, a short upper lip that does not rest closed (lip incompetence) and pregnancy rhinitis [1]. Wikipedia classifies mouth breathing as obstructive, habitual or anatomic [1]. Enlarged adenoids can obstruct airflow and are associated with snoring and sleep-disordered breathing [1].

sections.h: Proposed effects on the face and teeth
paras: Wikipedia lists anterior open bite, tongue thrusting, gingivitis and plaque among dental conditions associated with mouth breathing, and says chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth and contribute to a long, narrow face [1]. Support for these links comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual or cephalometric work [1].

The main approach described is treating any underlying nasal obstruction and building a habit of nasal breathing [1]. Orofacial myofunctional therapy adds exercises to optimise tongue placement and increase oropharyngeal muscle tone [3]. Mouth taping involves keeping the lips shut during sleep with a strip of surgical tape, and Wikipedia says its health effects have been little researched [1]. A May 2025 HealthDay report on a review of mouth taping carried the headline 'Little Benefit, Lots Of Risk', and Wikipedia notes that most mouth breathing is a response to nasal congestion [1][7].

A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine adult studies (120 patients) reported a fall in the mean apnea-hypopnea index from 24.5 to 12.3 events per hour, along with less snoring and lower sleepiness scores after myofunctional therapy [2]. A 2024 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials with 310 patients reported statistically significant improvements in apnea-hypopnea index, sleepiness and sleep-related quality of life [3].

A 2025 randomised trial compared a palatal crib alone with a crib plus brief OMT for anterior open bite in 32 patients, measuring tongue pressure and overbite change [5], and a 2016 pilot randomised study examined OMT in children with open bite and tongue dysfunction [6]. Reviews have also looked at OMT for tongue thrust habits and for ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) [8][9].

A looksmax.org thread describes OMT as the fundamentals behind tongue posture, mewing and jaw exercises and argues that an open mouth, low tongue and slack lips affect breathing, sleep, chewing and facial appearance [4]. In another thread a user describes a consultation at a clinic offering a jaw-growth device and facial exercises that compared the approach with mewing; the user questioned whether it could produce the jaw advancement they wanted [10]. Users also discuss nasal obstruction surgery and mouth taping [11][12].

Randomised trials and meta-analyses of myofunctional therapy exist for obstructive sleep apnea, open bite, tongue thrust and tongue-tie [2][3][5][6][8][9]. No study found tested mouth-breathing correction or OMT for changing adult facial structure or measured appearance as an outcome. Wikipedia reports that the evidence linking mouth breathing and facial growth is largely conceptual or based on limited cephalometric work [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, myofunctional therapy is discussed as the muscle-training foundation of tongue posture and mewing, and mouth taping and nasal breathing come up as sleep habits.
